Rules:
- One commitment per line.
- Write each as a verb phrase: an action followed by its object. For example: "raise the income tax threshold" or "build 300000 new homes".
- State each commitment at the level of a distinct policy action, not its implementation details. Do not subdivide a single commitment into steps.
- Include every commitment. Do not select, rank, prioritise, or judge importance.
- Use the text's own terms for policy objects. Do not substitute synonyms.
- Do not number the lines. No bullets, headings, preamble, or commentary.
- If the text states no policy commitments, output the single word NONE.

<text>
# Summary of 2005 Election Manifesto

This manifesto presents a vision for national governance centred on accountability, individual freedom, and reduced centralised control. The document outlines policies across several key areas.

## Economic Policy

The manifesto proposes reducing government spending by £12 billion annually through cutting bureaucratic posts, freezing civil service recruitment, and abolishing public bodies. Of these savings, £8 billion would reduce borrowing while £4 billion would fund tax cuts. The document advocates for lower taxes to promote enterprise and reward hard work, alongside reduced regulation on businesses.

For pensioners, proposals include halving council tax bills for households where all residents are over 65, increasing basic state pensions in line with earnings rather than prices, and creating Lifetime Savings Accounts with government contributions.

## Education

The manifesto prioritises school discipline, proposing that head teachers receive full control over admissions and expulsions. Disruptive pupils would attend special "Turnaround Schools." Teachers would receive protection from paperwork burdens and malicious allegations.

Funding would follow pupils directly, with schools gaining freedom to set their own priorities and budgets. The document proposes expanding school places by 600,000, offering vocational grants for 14-16 year olds, and guaranteeing two hours of after-school sport for every child. University tuition fees would be abolished.

## Healthcare

The manifesto commits to increasing NHS funding by £34 billion annually. Key reforms include abolishing centrally-set targets, reducing bureaucracy by cutting Primary Care Trusts and abolishing Strategic Health Authorities, and restoring matron positions with authority to close wards for cleaning.

Patients and GPs would gain the right to choose hospitals, with funding following patients directly.

## Law and Order

Proposals include recruiting 5,000 additional police officers annually, reducing paperwork, and introducing elected police commissioners for local accountability. The manifesto advocates ending early prison release, providing 20,000 extra prison places, and ensuring criminals serve full sentences.

Drug policy includes expanding treatment programmes to 25,000 residential rehabilitation places and reclassifying cannabis from Class C back to Class B.

## Immigration

The manifesto proposes establishing a British Border Control Police, implementing 24-hour port surveillance, and introducing an Australian-style points system for work permits. An annual limit on immigration would be set by Parliament, including a fixed quota for asylum seekers whose applications would be processed outside Britain.

## Constitutional Reform

Proposals include abolishing regional assemblies, reducing MPs by 20 per cent, strengthening parliamentary select committees, and ensuring English laws are decided by English votes only. The manifesto supports maintaining the union whilst respecting devolution arrangements.

## Foreign Policy and Defence

Military spending would increase by £2.7 billion for front-line services. The manifesto opposes joining the Euro and the EU Constitution, proposing a referendum within six months. It advocates restoring opt-outs from EU social policy and negotiating national control over fisheries.

On international development, the document commits to meeting the UN target of 0.7 per cent of national income on overseas aid by 2013.
